## Learning Objectives

By the end of today you will be able to:

::: {style="font-size: 0.80em;"}

- Explain the extra sum of squares principle and distinguish sequential (Type I) from partial (Type III) SS
- State why SSE and $R^2$ alone are insufficient model selection criteria
- Compute and interpret AIC and BIC as selection criteria
- Apply backward and forward selection and explain when each is appropriate

:::

---

## Extra Sum of Squares {background-color="#003660"}

---

## The Extra Sum of Squares — Definition

::: {style="font-size: 0.65em;"}

When more terms are added to a regression model, **SSR always increases** and **SSE always decreases** while SSTO remains unchanged.

::: {.fragment}
The extra sum of squares is the amount by which SSE drops (equivalently, the amount by which SSR rises) when a predictor is added to the model.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Comparing a **full model** $F$ to a **restricted model** $R$ (where $R$ is nested in $F$):

- $SSE(R)$ is always larger than $SSE(F)$
- Because SSTO is fixed, the extra SS can be written either way:

$$\underbrace{SSR(F) - SSR(R)}_{\text{extra SS}} = SSE(R) - SSE(F)$$
:::

:::

---

## The Extra Sum of Squares — F Test

::: {style="font-size: 0.80em;"}

To test whether the added predictors contribute significantly, we test:

$$H_0: \text{all coefficients added in } F \text{ are zero} \quad \text{vs.} \quad H_a: \text{at least one} \neq 0$$

Use the **F statistic**:

$$F^* = \frac{(SSE(R) - SSE(F))\,/\,(df_R - df_F)}{SSE(F)\,/\,df_F} \overset{H_0}{\sim} F_{df_R - df_F,\; df_F}$$

where $df_F$ and $df_R$ are degrees of freedom associated with $SSE(F)$ and $SSE(R)$.

::: {.fragment}
Reject $H_0$ if $F^* > F(1 - \alpha;\; df_R - df_F,\; df_F)$.
:::


:::

---

## Practice: Extra SS F Test 

::: {style="font-size: 0.75em;"}

Using `mtcars`, two models are fit:

- **Restricted model** $R$: `mpg ~ wt` — $SSE(R) = 278.32$, $df_R = 30$
- **Full model** $F$: `mpg ~ wt + hp + qsec` — $SSE(F) = 186.06$, $df_F = 28$

**(a)** What is the extra sum of squares? 

**(b)** Compute the F statistic $F^*$.

**(c)** The critical value is $F(0.95;\, 2,\, 28) = 3.34$. What do you conclude at $\alpha = 0.05$?

:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
countdown::countdown(
  minutes = 4,
  play_sound = TRUE,
  color_border              = "#FEBC11",
  color_text                = "#003660",
  color_running_background  = "#003660",
  color_running_text        = "#FFFFFF",
  color_finished_background = "#FEBC11",
  color_finished_text       = "#003660",
  font_size = "2em"
)
```

---

## Practice: Solution 

::: {style="font-size: 0.75em;"}

**(a)** Extra SS $= SSE(R) - SSE(F) = 278.32 - 186.06 = 92.26$


::: {.fragment}
**(b)**

$$F^* = \frac{(278.32 - 186.06)\,/\,(30 - 28)}{186.06\,/\,28} = \frac{92.26\,/\,2}{186.06\,/\,28} = \frac{46.13}{6.645} = 6.94$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
**(c)** Since $F^* = 6.94 > 3.34 = F(0.95;\, 2,\, 28)$, we reject $H_0$ at the $\alpha = 0.05$ significance level. There is significant evidence that `hp` and `qsec` together contribute to the model, given `wt` is already included.
:::

:::

---

## Sequential Sum of Squares (Type I) — Setup

::: {style="font-size: 0.63em;"}

Consider the full model $Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \beta_2 X_{i2} + \beta_3 X_{i3} + \varepsilon_i$. We introduce sequential SS by fitting three **nested models**:

$$\text{Model 1: } Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \varepsilon_i$$
$$\text{Model 2: } Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \beta_2 X_{i2} + \varepsilon_i$$
$$\text{Model 3: } Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \beta_2 X_{i2} + \beta_3 X_{i3} + \varepsilon_i$$

::: {.fragment}
Let $SSR(X_1)$, $SSR(X_1, X_2)$, $SSR(X_1, X_2, X_3)$ be the regression SS and $SSE(X_1)$, $SSE(X_1, X_2)$, $SSE(X_1, X_2, X_3)$ be the error SS for Models 1, 2, and 3. Define:

$$SSR(X_2 \mid X_1) = SSR(X_1, X_2) - SSR(X_1) = SSE(X_1) - SSE(X_1, X_2)$$
$$SSR(X_3 \mid X_1, X_2) = SSR(X_1, X_2, X_3) - SSR(X_1, X_2) = SSE(X_1, X_2) - SSE(X_1, X_2, X_3)$$
:::

:::

---

## Sequential Sum of Squares (Type I) — SSTO Decomposition

::: {style="font-size: 0.78em;"}

Fitting the full model (Model 3), SSTO decomposes as:

$$SSTO = SSR(X_1) + SSR(X_2 \mid X_1) + SSR(X_3 \mid X_1, X_2) + SSE(X_1, X_2, X_3)$$

::: {.fragment}

- $SSR(X_1)$: SS explained by $X_1$ alone
- $SSR(X_2 \mid X_1)$: extra SS due to adding $X_2$ to the model that already includes $X_1$
- $SSR(X_3 \mid X_1, X_2)$: extra SS due to adding $X_3$ to the model that already includes $X_1$ and $X_2$
:::


:::

---


## Partial Sum of Squares (Type III) — Motivation

::: {style="font-size: 0.58em;"}

**Type I (sequential):** each predictor's SS is conditioned on only the predictors entered *before* it in the model formula — **order matters!**.

::: {.fragment}
**Type III (partial):** each predictor's SS is conditioned on *all other* predictors simultaneously.**order never matters!**

$$SSR(X_k \mid \text{all other } X\text{'s})$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
For the full model with $X_1, X_2, X_3$, the partial SS for each predictor answers:

> *"How much does $X_k$ contribute, given that every other predictor is already in the model?"*

- $SSR(X_1 \mid X_2, X_3)$: drop $X_1$ from the full model $\rightarrow$ $H_0: \beta_1 = 0$
- $SSR(X_2 \mid X_1, X_3)$: drop $X_2$ from the full model $\rightarrow$ $H_0: \beta_2 = 0$
- $SSR(X_3 \mid X_1, X_2)$: drop $X_3$ from the full model $\rightarrow$ $H_0: \beta_3 = 0$
:::

:::

---

## Partial Sum of Squares (Type III) — in R

::: {style="font-size: 0.75em;"}

Use `car::Anova()` with `type = "III"` to compute partial SS for all predictors simultaneously:

:::

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true
#| message: false
library(car)
Anova(fit3, type = "III")
```

---

## Partial Sum of Squares (Type III) — Table & Properties

::: {style="font-size: 0.68em;"}

| Source | SS | $H_0$ tested |
|:-------|:---|:-------------|
| $X_1$ | $SSR(X_1 \mid X_2, X_3)$ | $\beta_1 = 0$ given $X_2, X_3$ in model |
| $X_2$ | $SSR(X_2 \mid X_1, X_3)$ | $\beta_2 = 0$ given $X_1, X_3$ in model |
| $X_3$ | $SSR(X_3 \mid X_1, X_2)$ | $\beta_3 = 0$ given $X_1, X_2$ in model |

::: {.fragment}
Key properties:

- **Order does not matter**. Each SS is conditioned on *all* other predictors
- These SS do **not** add up to $SSR(X_1, X_2, X_3)$ (unlike Type I SS)
:::


:::

## Practice: Sequential vs. Partial SS

::: {style="font-size: 0.75em;"}

Using `fit3 <- lm(mpg ~ hp + wt + qsec, data = mtcars)`:

**(a)** The sequential SS for `wt` is 252.6 (from `anova(fit1, fit2, fit3)`). The partial SS for `wt` is 183.1 (from `Anova(fit3, type="III")`). Write out the SS notation for each (e.g. $SSR(\texttt{wt} \mid \ldots)$). Then explain why the sequential SS is larger.

**(b)** For testing $H_0: \beta_{wt} = 0$ given `hp` and `qsec` are in the model, should you use sequential or partial SS? Why?

**(c)** True or false: changing the order of predictors in `lm(mpg ~ wt + hp + qsec)` changes the Type III SS.

:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
countdown::countdown(
  minutes = 5,
  play_sound = TRUE,
  color_border              = "#FEBC11",
  color_text                = "#003660",
  color_running_background  = "#003660",
  color_running_text        = "#FFFFFF",
  color_finished_background = "#FEBC11",
  color_finished_text       = "#003660",
  font_size = "2em"
)
```

---

## Practice: Solution

::: {style="font-size: 0.75em;"}

**(a)** Sequential: $SSR(\texttt{wt} \mid \texttt{hp})$ — conditions only on `hp`. 

Partial: $SSR(\texttt{wt} \mid \texttt{hp}, \texttt{qsec})$ — conditions on both `hp` and `qsec`.

 The sequential SS is larger because it measures the extra contribution of `wt` after just `hp`. The partial SS conditions on **both** `hp` and `qsec`, leaving less variation for `wt` to explain.

::: {.fragment}
**(b)** Use **partial (Type III) SS**. The null hypothesis $H_0: \beta_{wt} = 0$ tests whether `wt` contributes given `hp` and `qsec` are both in the model. This is exactly what partial SS measures.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**(c)** **False.** Type III SS are adjusted for all other predictors regardless of the order they appear in the formula. Reordering predictors in `lm()` does not change partial SS.
:::

:::

---

## Using SS to Make Model Decisions

::: {style="font-size: 0.60em;"}

**Extra SS F-test — does this group of predictors jointly improve the model?**

- Directly compare two nested models with `anova(fitR, fitF)`
- $F^* = \frac{(SSE(R) - SSE(F))\,/\,(df_R - df_F)}{SSE(F)\,/\,df_F}$; compare to $F(1-\alpha;\, df_R - df_F,\, df_F)$
- If $F^*$ is large $\rightarrow$ the predictors added in $F$ jointly improve the model
- Use when you want to test *multiple* predictors simultaneously (e.g. does adding `hp` and `qsec` help beyond `wt`?)


::: {.fragment}
**Partial SS (Type III) — should I keep this predictor?**

- Tests one predictor at a time: $H_0: \beta_k = 0$ given all others are in the model
- Compare $F^*$ to $F(1-\alpha;\, 1,\, n-p)$
- If $F^*$ is large $\rightarrow$ keep the predictor; it contributes beyond what the others already explain
- Use when deciding whether an individual predictor belongs in a model that already contains all other predictors


:::

:::

---

## Variable Selection {background-color="#003660"}

---

## Why Do We Need Variable Selection?

::: {style="font-size: 0.57em;"}

**Partial and sequential SS are hypothesis tests, not selection tools**

- They tell you whether a predictor is significant given what's already in the model
- They don't search over models or balance fit against complexity
- With many predictors, running individual tests on every possible combination is not an effective strategy

::: {.fragment}
**SSE and $R^2$ alone are also insufficient**

- **SSE** always decreases when predictors are added → always favors the largest model
- $R^2$ always increases when predictors are added → same problem
- **Adjusted $R^2$** penalizes for extra parameters but has no formal probabilistic interpretation

:::

::: {.fragment}
**What we need:** A systematic approach that balances goodness of fit against model complexity with formal statistical justification

::: {style="background-color: #f5f5f5; padding: 0.4em 1em; border-left: 4px solid #FEBC11; margin-top: 0.3em;"}
With $p - 1$ candidate predictors there are $2^{p-1}$ possible models. **AIC** and **BIC** give us principled criteria for choosing among them.
:::
:::

:::

---

## AIC and BIC 

::: {style="font-size: 0.75em;"}

AIC and BIC are **model comparison criteria**. They are numbers you compute for a fitted model that balance fit against complexity. They are not selection procedures themselves; they are the *metrics* that selection procedures use.

::: {.fragment}
- **As a criterion**: compute AIC (or BIC) for any fitted model (lower is better)
- **As the basis for selection**: compare values across candidate models and pick the smallest; 
:::

::: {.fragment}
Both take the form: **goodness-of-fit term + complexity penalty**. Adding a useless predictor reduces the fit term only slightly but increases the penalty, so the total goes up.
:::

:::

---

## AIC and BIC — Formulas {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size: 0.68em;"}

::: {style="background-color: #f5f5f5; padding: 0.4em 1em; border-left: 4px solid #FEBC11;"}
**AIC** *(Akaike Information Criterion)* estimates out-of-sample prediction error and penalizes each parameter by 2.

$$\text{AIC} = n \log\!\left(\frac{SSE}{n}\right) + 2p$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {style="background-color: #f5f5f5; padding: 0.4em 1em; border-left: 4px solid #003660; margin-top: 0.4em;"}
**BIC** *(Bayesian Information Criterion)* implements a heavier penalty than AIC when $n > 7$, favoring smaller models.

$$\text{BIC} = n \log\!\left(\frac{SSE}{n}\right) + \log(n) \cdot p$$
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Select the model with the smallest AIC (or BIC).**

| Criterion | Penalty | Tendency |
|:----------|:-------:|:---------|
| AIC | $2p$ | Favors slightly larger models |
| BIC | $\log(n)\cdot p$ | Favors smaller models |

:::

:::

---


## Stepwise Procedures 

::: {style="font-size: 0.63em;"}

With $p - 1$ candidate predictors, there are $2^{p-1}$ possible models. For large $p$, we can use stepwise methods to select predictors for our model. **Stepwise methods** are greedy approximations that search the model space one predictor at a time.

::: {.fragment}
All stepwise methods use AIC as the decision criterion at each step (or BIC if `k = log(n)`). 

| Method | Starting point | Move at each step |
|:-------|:--------------|:------------------|
| Backward elimination | Full model | Remove the predictor that most lowers AIC |
| Forward addition | Intercept only | Add the predictor that most lowers AIC |
:::


:::

---

## Backward Elimination

::: {style="font-size: 0.82em;"}

Start with the full model.

 At each step:

- Remove the predictor whose removal most lowers AIC 
- Stop when removing anything would increase AIC


::: {.fragment}
In R:
```r
(fit_back <- step(full_model, direction = "backward"))
```
:::

:::

---


## Forward Addition

::: {style="font-size: 0.82em;"}

Start with the intercept-only model.

 At each step: 
 
 - Add the predictor whose addition most lowers AIC
 - Stop when adding anything would increase AIC

::: {.fragment}
In R:
```r
(fit_fwd <- step(lm(mpg ~ 1, data = mtcars), scope = formula(full_model), direction = "forward"))
```
The `scope` argument tells `step()` the largest model it is allowed to consider.
:::

:::

## Practice: Stepwise Selection 

::: {style="font-size: 0.65em;"}

Backward stepwise AIC was run on `mpg ~ hp + wt + qsec + am`. Here is the output:

```
Start:  AIC=61.52
mpg ~ hp + wt + qsec + am

       Df Sum of Sq    RSS    AIC
- hp    1     9.219 169.29 61.307
<none>              160.07 61.515
- qsec  1    20.225 180.29 63.323
- am    1    25.993 186.06 64.331
- wt    1    78.494 238.56 72.284

Step:  AIC=61.31
mpg ~ wt + qsec + am

       Df Sum of Sq    RSS    AIC
<none>              169.29 61.307
- am    1    26.178 195.46 63.908
- qsec  1   109.034 278.32 75.217
- wt    1   183.347 352.63 82.790
```

**(a)** At Step 1, which predictor is removed and why?

**(b)** Why does the algorithm stop after Step 2?

**(c)** What is the final selected model?

:::


## Practice: Solution 

::: {style="font-size: 0.75em;"}

**(a)** `hp` is removed — it has the lowest AIC (61.307) among all removal options, and that AIC is lower than keeping the current model (`<none>` = 61.515). Removing `hp` improves the model.

::: {.fragment}
**(b)** At Step 2, the AIC of `<none>` (61.307) is lower than the AIC of removing any remaining predictor (`am` = 63.908, `qsec` = 75.217, `wt` = 82.790). No removal helps, so the algorithm stops.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**(c)** The final model is `mpg ~ wt + qsec + am`.
:::

:::

## Summary

::: {style="font-size: 0.63em;"}

::: {.incremental}

- **Extra SS F-test:** compares a restricted model $R$ to a full model $F$; $F^* = \frac{(SSE(R)-SSE(F))/(df_R-df_F)}{SSE(F)/df_F}$; tests whether the added predictors jointly contribute

- **Sequential SS (Type I):** each predictor's SS is conditioned on predictors entered before it so order matters; computed with `anova()`

- **Partial SS (Type III):** each predictor's SS is conditioned on all other predictors simultaneously so order never matters; computed with `Anova(..., type="III")`; 

- **Why variable selection?** SSE and $R^2$ always improve with more predictors; partial/sequential SS are hypothesis tests, not search tools; we need criteria that balance fit against complexity

- **AIC and BIC:** both penalize model complexity — $\text{AIC} = n\log(SSE/n) + 2p$, $\text{BIC} = n\log(SSE/n) + \log(n)\cdot p$; BIC penalizes more heavily and favors smaller models; lower is better

- **Stepwise selection:** backward starts from the full model and removes; forward starts from intercept-only and adds; at each step, compare candidate AIC values to `<none>` (current model) and stop when no change helps

:::

:::
